lesson.title: The Overtones Hiding Inside Every Non-Sinusoidal Wave
lesson.summary: Harmonics are frequency components located at exact integer multiples of a periodic signal's fundamental frequency, and the particular mix of harmonics present, not just the fundamental, is what gives a non-sinusoidal waveform its characteristic shape.
lesson.body:
The nth harmonic of a periodic signal is a frequency component located at exactly n times the fundamental frequency, n x f0, for whole numbers n of 2 or greater (the fundamental itself is occasionally called the first harmonic, n = 1). A pure sine wave is the one special case with no harmonics at all, just its single fundamental component. Any periodic signal that departs from a pure sine shape, a square wave, a triangle wave, a sawtooth wave, a distorted audio signal, carries energy at harmonic frequencies in addition to its fundamental, and it is precisely that extra harmonic content that makes the waveform look like something other than a smooth sine curve.

Take the square wave clock signal from the previous chapter, with fundamental frequency f0 = 1 kHz (period 1 ms). Its harmonic frequencies fall at exact multiples of 1 kHz: the 2nd harmonic sits at 2 x 1 kHz = 2 kHz, the 3rd harmonic at 3 x 1 kHz = 3 kHz, and the 5th harmonic at 5 x 1 kHz = 5 kHz. An ideal square wave has a well-known property, confirmed by the Fourier series worked out in the next chapter: it contains only odd-numbered harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, and so on) and no even-numbered harmonics at all. That means the 3 kHz and 5 kHz components are present with real, measurable amplitude in this clock signal's spectrum, while the 2 kHz component is entirely absent.

Harmonics are not just a mathematical curiosity, they connect directly back to the non-ideal op-amp behavior covered earlier in this chapter sequence. A digital clock's sharp rising and falling edges contain meaningful energy in harmonics reaching far above the clock's own fundamental frequency, often into the tens or hundreds of megahertz for a fast clock. Any amplifier stage handling that signal needs bandwidth, set by its gain-bandwidth product, and slew rate that comfortably cover those higher harmonics, not just the fundamental. Fall short on either spec and the higher harmonics get attenuated or slew-limited away, which is exactly what rounds off a square wave's sharp corners into something closer to a rounded pulse or even a sine wave.
